## How hand hygiene breaks the chain of infection

- The chain of infection describes how infection spreads through six links:
  - Infectious agent
  - Reservoir
  - Portal of exit
  - Mode of transmission
  - Portal of entry
  - Susceptible host
- If any link in the chain is removed or neutralized, transmission of infection will not occur.
- Routine hygienic practices, standard precautions, and transmission-based precautions are used to break the chain of transmission.
- Health care providers’ hands are the most common mode of transmission of microorganisms.
- Hands can transfer microorganisms indirectly:
  - From a client
  - From a client’s personal items
  - From medical equipment
  - From the client’s surrounding environment
  - To the client
  - To another client
  - To the health care worker
  - To equipment
  - To a new environment
- Consistent and effective hand hygiene breaks the chain of transmission by removing, killing, or destroying microorganisms or visible contaminants from the hands.
- Hand hygiene has two techniques:
  - Handwashing with soap and water
  - Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR), also called hand hygiene gel or hand sanitizer

## Moments when hand hygiene prevents transmission

Health care workers should perform hand hygiene:

- Immediately before touching a patient
- Before performing an aseptic task, such as emptying urine from a Foley catheter bag
- Before moving from a soiled body site to a clean body site
- After touching a patient or the patient’s immediate environment
- After contact with blood, body fluids, or contaminated surfaces, with or without gloves
- Immediately after glove removal

Hand hygiene should also be performed immediately after contact with respiratory secretions.

## Standard precautions related to hand hygiene

Standard precautions are used during client care when contact or potential contact with blood or body fluids may occur. They are based on the principle that all of the following may contain transmissible infectious agents:

- Blood
- Body fluids, except sweat
- Nonintact skin
- Mucous membranes

Standard precautions include:

- Using proper hand hygiene at the appropriate times
- Using personal protective equipment whenever exposure to infectious agents may occur
- Implementing respiratory hygiene
- Properly cleaning and sanitizing the environment, equipment, and devices
- Handling laundry safely
- Using transmission-based precautions when indicated

## Handwashing with soap and water

- Handwashing physically removes microorganisms from the hands.
- Soap and water must be used when hands:
  - Are visibly soiled
  - Have been exposed to blood or body fluids
  - Have been exposed to *norovirus*
  - Have been exposed to *C. difficile*
  - Have been exposed to *Bacillus anthracis*
- The mechanical action of lathering and scrubbing with soap for a minimum of **20 seconds** is vital for removing these microorganisms.
- The entire handwashing procedure should last **40 to 60 seconds**.
- Water alone is not suitable for cleaning soiled hands.
- Soap must be rubbed on all surfaces of both hands, followed by thorough rinsing and drying.
- Friction and rubbing are required to remove transient bacteria, oil, and debris.
- Multistep rubbing techniques are required to promote coverage of all hand surfaces.

### Handwashing steps

- Wet hands with warm or cold running water and apply facility-approved soap.
- Lather hands by rubbing them together with the soap.
- Clean:
  - Palms
  - Fingers
  - Between the fingers
  - Backs of the hands and fingers
  - Fingertips
  - Thumbs
- Scrub thoroughly for at least **20 seconds**.
- Rinse hands well under clean, running water.
- Dry hands from fingers to wrists using a clean towel or disposable toweling.
- Use a clean paper towel to shut off the faucet.

### Handwashing skill-checklist details

- Keep hands and forearms lower than the elbows.
- Avoid splashing water on the uniform.
- Apply a palm-sized amount of hand soap.
- Use plenty of lather and friction for at least **15 seconds** while:
  - Rubbing hands palm to palm
  - Rubbing the backs of the right and left hands with fingers interlaced
  - Rubbing palm to palm with fingers interlaced
  - Performing rotational rubbing of the left and right thumbs
  - Rubbing fingertips against the palm of the opposite hand
  - Rubbing the wrists
- Repeat the rubbing sequence at least two times.
- Keep fingertips pointing downward.
- Clean under fingernails with a disposable nail cleaner, if applicable.
- Wash for a minimum of **20 seconds**.
- Rinse with fingertips pointing down so water runs off the fingertips.
- Do not shake water from the hands.
- Do not lean against the sink or touch the inside of the sink.
- Dry hands thoroughly from fingers to wrists with a paper towel or air dryer.
- Use a new paper towel to turn off the water.

## Alcohol-based hand rub

- ABHR is the preferred method for hand hygiene when soap-and-water handwashing is not required.
- ABHR reduces the number of transient microorganisms on the hands.
- ABHR is more effective for preventing healthcare-acquired infections caused by:
  - Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA)
  - Vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE)
- The agency-provided ABHR should contain **70–90% alcohol**.
- ABHR should be performed in front of the client before care begins and at the end of the interaction.
- ABHR:
  - Kills the majority of microorganisms, including viruses, from hands
  - Requires less time than soap-and-water handwashing
  - Provides better skin tolerability
  - Reduces skin irritation because it contains emollients
  - Is available at the point of care

### When not to use ABHR

Do not use ABHR when:

- Hands are visibly soiled
- Hands have been exposed to blood or body fluids
- The client is suspected of having or confirmed to have *C. difficile*
- The client is suspected of having or confirmed to have *norovirus*
- The client is suspected of having or confirmed to have *Bacillus

## How hand hygiene breaks the chain of infection

### Chain-of-infection mechanism

- Pathogens are continually introduced into homes and community settings by:
  - People who may be infected or asymptomatic.
  - Food.
  - Domestic animals.
  - Sometimes water or air.
- Sites where stagnant water accumulates—including sinks, toilets, waste pipes, cleaning cloths, and face cloths—can support microbial growth and become reservoirs of infection.
- The chain of infection involves transmission from an original source to a new recipient.
- Although the exit and entry of pathogens from and into the body can be limited, the part of the chain over which people have the most control is the “spread of pathogens.”
- Good hygiene can interrupt this spread, including:
  - Hand hygiene.
  - Cleaning and disinfecting contaminated environmental surfaces.
- The critical control points for breaking the chain of infection are:
  - Hands.
  - Hand-contact surfaces.
  - Food-contact surfaces.
  - Cleaning cloths.
  - Other cleaning utensils.
- Hands are probably the single most important transmission route for gastrointestinal, respiratory tract, and skin infections because they come into direct contact with portals of entry:
  - Mouth.
  - Nose.
  - Conjunctiva of the eyes.
- Hands are therefore described as a key “last line of defense” against infection.

### Examples of transmission pathways interrupted by hand hygiene

- **Gastrointestinal infection:**
  - Contaminated food → food-contact surface → hands → mouth of a recipient.
  - Infected person or carrier → hands → food → mouth of a recipient.
  - Contaminated surface → hands → mouth.
- **Respiratory infection:**
  - Infected respiratory secretions → hands or surfaces → eyes or nose.
  - Rhinovirus and respiratory syncytial virus can be deposited into the front of the nose or into the eye, where they pass down the lacrimal duct.
- **Skin and wound infection:**
  - Person carrying or infected with *Staphylococcus aureus* or MRSA → hands → wound or damaged skin of a recipient.
- Hand hygiene may be a sufficient cause of transmission in some situations, such as:
  - An MRSA carrier → hands → wound of a recipient.
- In other situations, transmission involves several component causes, such as:
  - Contaminated food → food-contact surface → hands → mouth.

### Why small amounts of contamination matter

| Pathogen | Infectious dose or relevant figure |
|---|---:|
| *Salmonella* species | Up to 10⁶ organisms; may be as low as 10–100 cells |
| *Campylobacter* species | 500 organisms can result in human illness |
| *E. coli* O157 | May be as little as 10 cells; one outbreak reported a median dose of fewer than 100 organisms per hamburger |
| Norovirus | 10–100 units or even less |
| Rotavirus | May be as few as 10 particles |
| Respiratory syncytial virus | 100–640 TCID₅₀ by intranasal inoculation |
| Rhinovirus | 0.032–0.4 TCID₅₀; also cited as 1–10 TCID₅₀ |
| Influenza | 2–790 TCID₅₀ by intranasal inoculation |
| Parainfluenza | 1.5–80 TCID₅₀ by intranasal inoculation |
| *S. aureus* on healthy skin | Up to 10⁶ cells may be required to produce pus |
| *S. aureus* on occluded or traumatized skin | As little as 10² cells may be sufficient |

- TCID₅₀ means tissue culture infective dose.
- A small number of organisms transferred from contaminated hands to the mouth, nose, eyes, food, or a wound can therefore be relevant to infection risk.

### How contamination reaches and spreads through hands

- Children frequently touch their mouths:
  - Children under 24 months: 81 mouthing events per hour.
  - Children over 24 months: approximately 42 mouthing events per hour.
- Touching lettuce for 10 seconds with contaminated finger pads transferred:
  - 9.2% of hepatitis A virus.
  - 18% of feline calicivirus, used as a surrogate for norovirus.
  - Based on the hepatitis A virus load in feces, approximately 1,300 viral particles were transferred to lettuce.
- In a model domestic kitchen, 29% of food-preparation sessions using chicken contaminated with *Campylobacter* resulted in positive isolations from:
  - Prepared salads.
  - Cleaning materials.
  - Food-contact surfaces.
- Transfer from contaminated fingertips to the lip area was:
  - *Micrococcus luteus*: 40.99%.
  - *Serratia rubidea*: 33.97%.
  - Bacteriophage PRD-1: 33.90%.
- Following a handshake with a volunteer whose hands had been contaminated by touching a virus-contaminated door handle, successive transmission was followed through the sixth person.
- Norovirus transferred from contaminated fingers to melamine surfaces and then to:
  - Taps.
  - Door handles.
  - Telephone receivers.
- Contaminated fingers sequentially transferred norovirus to up to 7 clean surfaces.
- Transfer efficiencies from contaminated surfaces to hands included:
  - Telephone receiver: 38%–65%.
  - Faucet: 27%–40%.
- Influenza virus was detected on:
  - 23% of sampled day-care-centre surfaces during autumn 2003.
  - 53% of sampled day-care-centre surfaces during spring.
  - 59% of surfaces sampled in March in 5 homes containing an influenza-infected child.
  - 0% of surfaces in 3 homes where all household members were healthy.
- In the homes with an influenza-infected child, influenza virus was recovered most frequently from telephone receivers, at 80%, and least frequently from computer keyboards, at 40%.

### How hand hygiene removes or kills pathogens

Hand decontamination can be achieved by:

- **Handwashing with soap or detergent and water:**
  - Physically dislodges organisms.
  - Rubbing maximizes the release of microbes from the skin.
  - Rinsing washes organisms away from the hands.
- **Alcohol-based hand sanitizers (ABHS):**
  - Kill microbes in situ.
  - Contain ethanol, 1-propanol, 2-propanol, or combinations.
  - Their antimicrobial activity is attributed to denaturation of proteins.
- **Using procedures in sequence:**
  - Handwashing followed by ABHS can increase the log reduction of contamination in increased-risk situa

- Appropriate hand hygiene is described as the single most effective action to stop the spread of infection, when integrated with other critical measures.
- Appropriate hand hygiene prevents up to **50% of avoidable infections acquired during health care delivery**, including infections affecting the health workforce.
- The WHO multimodal hand hygiene improvement strategy has led to:
  - Significant improvement in key hand hygiene indicators.
  - A reduction in health care-associated infections (HAIs).
  - A reduction in antimicrobial resistance.
  - Substantial help in stopping outbreaks.
- Appropriate hand hygiene reduces the risk of **SARS-CoV-2**, the virus that causes COVID-19, infection among health workers.
- Effective hand hygiene is a key measure for:
  - Preventing the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
  - Safe COVID-19 vaccination.
  - Reducing the burden of health care-associated infections.
  - Reducing the spread of antimicrobial resistance.
- Implementing hand hygiene policies can generate economic savings averaging **16 times the cost** of implementation.
- Hand hygiene compliance is recommended as a key performance indicator for infection prevention and control programmes, patient safety and quality of health services worldwide.
- Hand hygiene facilities at the point of care are important because **1 in 3 health care facilities** lack them.
- Compliance with hand hygiene best practices is only around **9%** during care of critically ill patients in low-income countries.
- Hand hygiene compliance levels in high-income countries rarely exceed **70%**.
- Globally, out of every **100 patients**, **7 in developed countries** and **15 in developing countries** acquire at least one HAI in acute care hospitals.

## How hand hygiene breaks the chain of infection

- Hand hygiene is a simple, low-cost infection prevention and control intervention performed at **critical moments**.
- Hand hygiene at key moments helps prevent:
  - Health care-associated infections (HAIs)
  - Microbial transmission
  - Spread of multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs)
  - Spread of resistant organisms
- The page identifies the **absence of, or inadequate, hand hygiene practices at key moments** as a critical defect in the quality of care.
- Hand hygiene is described as a building block for infection prevention and control because it:
  - Reduces transmission of microorganisms during clinical care.
  - Supports prevention of HAIs and antimicrobial resistance.
  - Can contribute to reduced infection rates when included in guidelines, education, monitoring, feedback, multimodal strategies, and adequate access to hand hygiene products.
- Hand hygiene multimodal improvement strategies were reported to improve practices and prevent microbial transmission and infections.
- Hand hygiene strategies should explain how hand hygiene prevents MDRO transmission in the context of real-life clinical workflow.
- Hand hygiene resources need to be available at the point of care. The page states that without hand hygiene resources, the spread of resistant organisms will occur.
- Factors identified as affecting hand hygiene compliance included:
  - Accessibility to handrub
  - Role models
  - Personal sense of responsibility
  - Emotional involvement
  - Workload
  - Staffing levels
  - Access to hand hygiene facilities
- Placement of handrub dispensers at the point of care was identified as a determinant of hand hygiene compliance.
- Limited access to hand hygiene facilities was described as a source of frustration for health care workers.
- Hand hygiene monitoring, audit, and feedback can improve hand hygiene behaviour and help prevent the spread of resistant organisms.

## Specific figures and outcomes

- **85% significant reduction in CAUTIs:** A study implementing hospital-wide catheter guidelines and measures aimed at early catheter removal reported an **85% significant reduction** in the number of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), together with increased hand hygiene compliance.
- **Hand hygiene compliance increase following monitoring and feedback:** In a 12-month multicentre collaboration in the USA:
  - Intensive care unit (ICU) compliance increased from **26% to 37%**.
  - Non-ICU compliance increased from **36% to 51%**.
- **Evidence involving hand hygiene:** **51 of 116 high-quality papers (44%)** used as primary evidence for six of the eight core components investigated hand hygiene as part of infection prevention and control interventions.
- In the review of multimodal strategies:
  - **28 studies** reported improved hand hygiene compliance among health care workers.
  - An additional **27 studies** reported that multimodal strategies involving education, system change, surveillance, and feedback helped improve hand hygiene compliance.
- In a hand hygiene education review:
  - Three studies reported that multidisciplinary focus groups engaging frontline health care workers contributed to improved hand hygiene compliance and reduced HAI rates.
  - Bedside teaching was associated with increased correct hand hygiene performance and reduced catheter-related bloodstream infections.
- In a monitoring and feedback study, feedback on hand hygiene behaviour produced higher odds of hand hygiene compliance in acute-care wards for elderly patients.

- Hand hygiene is described as a cornerstone of infection prevention.
- Poor hand-hygiene adherence among healthcare workers undermines infection-prevention efforts and contributes to the persistence of healthcare-associated infections.
- Knowledge gaps and misconceptions regarding the WHO “Five Moments” for hand hygiene and the appropriate use of gloves were identified as contributing challenges.
- **Glove-use misconception:** 48.2% of respondents believed that hand hygiene was unnecessary when gloves were worn. This indicates that wearing gloves does not eliminate the need for hand hygiene.
- 86% of respondents were aware of the WHO “Five Moments,” but detailed understanding was inconsistent.
- The mean hand-hygiene knowledge score was **71%**, categorized as **moderate**.
- The study assessed knowledge with a **33-item** tool:
  - Good: **>75%**
  - Moderate: **50–74%**
  - Poor: **<50%**
- Qualitative findings identified limited protocol adherence, reliance on routine habits rather than guidelines, insufficient training, inadequate institutional support, and misconceptions about glove use as factors undermining hand-hygiene knowledge and practice.
- Targeted and continuous education, visible hand-hygiene instructions, stronger Infection Prevention and Control committees, and improved institutional support were identified as necessary to foster effective hand-hygiene practices and reduce healthcare-associated infections.
- No misconceptions specifically attributed to school or college students are stated on the page.

## How hand hygiene breaks the chain of infection

- Microorganisms can be transferred from contaminated environmental surfaces and noncritical equipment to a susceptible patient through:
  - Direct contact by the susceptible patient.
  - Contact by healthcare personnel, caretakers, or visitors, followed by transfer to the susceptible patient.

- Contaminated hands or gloves of healthcare personnel, caretakers, and visitors can:
  - Transfer microorganisms from contaminated surfaces to susceptible patients.
  - Continue to spread microorganisms around the environment.
  - Contaminate environmental surfaces after contact with a colonized or infected patient.

- Proper hand hygiene, preceded by glove removal when applicable, can break this chain of transmission.

- Proper hand hygiene and environmental cleaning can prevent transfer of microorganisms:
  - To healthcare personnel, caretakers, and visitors.
  - To susceptible patients.

## Figures and specific data

- Healthcare-associated infection rates are approximately:
  - **15 out of every 100 patients** in limited-resource healthcare settings.
  - **7 out of every 100 patients** in high-resource healthcare settings.

- Some healthcare-associated pathogens can survive on environmental surfaces for months:
  - *Acinetobacter* species: up to **5 months**.
  - *Klebsiella* species: up to **30 months**.

- Actual survival times in healthcare settings vary considerably according to:
  - Temperature.
  - Humidity.
  - Surface type.
